_readme: Linux Guardian -- linux/incidents.json                        (Phase 8)
THE INCIDENT REGISTRY. This file is the answer to a problem Phase 7 ended
with: a single CPU load produced FOUR separate CRITICAL anomalies --
load_1min, load_5min, load_per_core and cpu_idle_ticks -- because they are
four symptoms of one thing. Four alarms for one event is how an alerting
system teaches people to ignore it (brief section 12).
Each entry below names a set of metrics that are symptoms of the SAME
underlying condition. When several of them go abnormal together, the
incident engine raises ONE incident and lists the symptoms inside it.
WHY A DECLARED TABLE AND NOT AUTOMATIC CORRELATION.
Statistical correlation between metrics is learnable in principle and
meaningless here in practice: it needs weeks of labelled data this
machine does not have, and it would produce groupings nobody could
defend in a viva. This file is a human writing down what is already
known -- that the load averages and CPU idle time describe one thing --
which is honest, reviewable, and correct on the first day.
WHY IT IS SHAPED LIKE actions.json.
Same reason, same pattern: a registry is an ALLOW-LIST. An incident type
that is not written here cannot be raised, and -- the part that matters --
'recommended_actions' may only name ids that already exist in
actions.json. guardian_incidents.check_registry() verifies that at load
time, so the incident engine can never recommend an action the action
registry has not already approved. The engine proposes; the registry
remains the boundary.
FIELDS
id                  stable identifier, used in the fingerprint
title               what a human sees in the list
category            one of SYSTEM PERFORMANCE NETWORK SERVICE PROCESS
SECURITY (brief section 21)
component           what is affected: cpu memory disk network processes
services
base_severity       how serious this KIND of event is, before anything
observed adjusts it. See guardian_risk.assess_severity.
impact              0..1, how much of this machine depends on the
component. A judgement, written down once, arguable.
security_relevant   true if this type is a security signal, which raises
severity and feeds the risk score
symptoms            the metric names that belong to this condition
primary             the one symptom whose numbers head the description
description         one sentence explaining what the condition means
investigate         which read-only action to run for root-cause evidence
recommended_actions ids from actions.json. RECOMMENDED, never executed
here -- Phase 3's approval path still applies in full.
Keys beginning with '_' are documentation and are stripped before the
program sees the file, exactly as in actions.json.

incidents.title: CPU saturation
incidents.description: The machine is doing far more work than it usually does. Everything on it will feel slower.
incidents._comment: This is the group that motivated the whole file: the four CRITICAL findings at the end of Phase 7 are all in here. cpu_idle_ticks is a counter, so the detector analyses its RATE -- idle ticks per second falls as the machine gets busier, which is why a 'below baseline' finding on it belongs to a saturation incident.

incidents.title: Memory pressure
incidents.description: Available memory is falling, or the machine has started paging to disk.
incidents._comment: swap_used_percent is in the same group as memory_used_percent on purpose. Swap climbing while RAM looks comfortable is the signature of memory pressure that a RAM percentage alone hides, and they are one condition, not two.

incidents.title: Disk filling or saturated
incidents.description: The root filesystem is filling up, or the disk is busier than it normally is.
incidents._comment: Capacity and throughput are grouped together because a human investigating either one wants to see the other: a disk that is both filling AND busy is a backup or a runaway log, and the two numbers together say which.

incidents.title: systemd unit failure
incidents.description: One or more systemd units have entered the failed state.
incidents._comment: base_severity is HIGH rather than MEDIUM because failed_units is not a measurement that drifted -- it is the machine's own report that something is broken. heal_service is RECOMMENDED here and nothing more: it still has to pass the action registry, PROTECTED_SERVICES, HEALABLE_SERVICES and the confirm step before it can run.

incidents.title: Process or descriptor leak
incidents.description: The number of processes, zombies or open file descriptors is climbing and not coming back down.
incidents._comment: These four are the failures that no CPU, RAM or disk gauge will ever show you: the machine looks idle right up to the moment everything starts failing with 'Too many open files'.

incidents.title: Unusual network activity
incidents.description: Traffic or connection counts are well outside this machine's usual pattern.
incidents._comment: base_severity is LOW because a traffic spike is usually somebody downloading something. It is still worth an incident -- section 20 of the brief asks for connection-spike detection -- but starting it at LOW is what stops the list filling with red every time the VM updates its packages.

incidents.title: Network interface errors
incidents.description: The interface is reporting packet errors, which usually means a driver or link problem rather than load.
incidents._comment: Kept separate from network_anomaly deliberately. Errors and volume are unrelated problems with unrelated causes, and grouping them would mean a busy afternoon and a failing cable produced the same incident.

incidents.title: Listening port change
incidents.description: The number of sockets this machine is listening on has changed. Every listening socket is a door.
incidents._comment: The clearest example of why an anomaly baseline beats a threshold. There is no correct NUMBER of listening ports to alarm on -- it depends entirely on the machine. What is always interesting is that the number CHANGED, and only a baseline can notice that.

incidents.title: Unusual login activity
incidents.description: The number of logged-in sessions is outside this machine's usual pattern.
incidents._comment: base_severity LOW, but security_relevant true, so guardian_risk raises it a step and weights it in the risk score. On a single-user demo VM a second session really is worth a line; on a shared server this entry would be retuned rather than removed.

incidents.title: Unclassified metric anomaly
incidents.description: A metric is behaving abnormally but does not belong to any declared incident type.
incidents._comment: THE CATCH-ALL, and it exists so that nothing is ever silently dropped. A metric added to metrics.sh but not yet placed in a group above still produces a visible, low-severity incident naming itself, rather than vanishing because no rule matched it. An empty 'symptoms' list is what marks this entry as the fallback; the engine never matches it by symptom.
